studyMetadata.description:
Most people, at some point, ask the big questions. Where did everything come from? Does my life have any meaning? Is there a God – and if so, what is He like? Genesis doesn’t ease into these questions slowly. It answers them from its very first sentence.
“In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.” (Genesis 1:1, NET)
Before anything else existed – before people, before the world – God was already there. He is not part of creation. He does not depend on anything. Everything begins with Him.

chapters.chapterTitle: In the Beginning – God the Creator

elements.text:
Most people, at some point, ask the big questions. Where did everything come from? Does my life have any meaning? Is there a God – and if so, what is He like? Genesis answers from its first sentence: “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.” (Genesis 1:1, NET) Before anything else existed, God was already there. He is not part of creation, and He does not depend on it. Everything begins with Him.

Tap each Bible reference to read the passage, write your own answer, then tap Check [[icon:localValidate]] to see how it compares. After you have answered, Main point [[icon:mainPoint]] shows the key idea.

1In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.

2Now the earth was without shape and empty, and darkness was over the surface of the watery deep, but the Spirit of God was moving over the surface of the water. 3God said, “Let there be light.” And there was light! 4God saw that the light was good, so God separated the light from the darkness. 5God called the light “day” and the darkness “night.” There was evening, and there was morning, marking the first day.

6God said, “Let there be an expanse in the midst of the waters and let it separate water from water.” 7So God made the expanse and separated the water under the expanse from the water above it. It was so. 8God called the expanse “sky.” There was evening, and there was morning, a second day.

9God said, “Let the water under the sky be gathered to one place and let dry ground appear.” It was so. 10God called the dry ground “land” and the gathered waters he called “seas.” God saw that it was good.

11God said, “Let the land produce vegetation: plants yielding seeds and trees on the land bearing fruit with seed in it, according to their kinds.” It was so. 12The land produced vegetation—plants yielding seeds according to their kinds, and trees bearing fruit with seed in it according to their kinds. God saw that it was good. 13There was evening, and there was morning, a third day.

14God said, “Let there be lights in the expanse of the sky to separate the day from the night, and let them be signs to indicate seasons and days and years, 15and let them serve as lights in the expanse of the sky to give light on the earth.” It was so. 16God made two great lights —the greater light to rule over the day and the lesser light to rule over the night. He made the stars also. 17God placed the lights in the expanse of the sky to shine on the earth, 18to preside over the day and the night, and to separate the light from the darkness. God saw that it was good. 19There was evening, and there was morning, a fourth day.

20God said, “Let the water swarm with swarms of living creatures and let birds fly above the earth across the expanse of the sky.” 21God created the great sea creatures and every living and moving thing with which the water swarmed, according to their kinds, and every winged bird according to its kind. God saw that it was good. 22God blessed them and said, “Be fruitful and multiply and fill the water in the seas, and let the birds multiply on the earth.” 23There was evening, and there was morning, a fifth day.

24God said, “Let the land produce living creatures according to their kinds: cattle, creeping things, and wild animals, each according to its kind.” It was so. 25God made the wild animals according to their kinds, the cattle according to their kinds, and all the creatures that creep along the ground according to their kinds. God saw that it was good.

26Then God said, “Let us make humankind in our image, after our likeness, so they may rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of the air, over the cattle, and over all the earth, and over all the creatures that move on the earth.”

27God created humankind in his own image,
in the image of God he created them,
male and female he created them.

28God blessed them and said to them, “Be fruitful and multiply! Fill the earth and subdue it! Rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of the air and every creature that moves on the ground.” 29Then God said, “I now give you every seed-bearing plant on the face of the entire earth and every tree that has fruit with seed in it. They will be yours for food. 30And to all the animals of the earth, and to every bird of the air, and to all the creatures that move on the ground—everything that has living breath in it—I give every green plant for food.” It was so.

31God saw all that he had made—and it was very good! There was evening, and there was morning, the sixth day.

elements.passageText:
1In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.

2Now the earth was without shape and empty, and darkness was over the surface of the watery deep, but the Spirit of God was moving over the surface of the water.

elements.question: What does verse 1 tell us about who God is in relation to the heavens and the earth?
elements.questionHint:
Notice who is acting in verse 1.
Notice what is acted upon.
elements.sampleAnswer: God is the Creator: He is the one who acts, and the heavens and the earth are what He acts upon. The verse begins with God, so He is already there before anything else exists and is not part of what He made. Verse 2 describes an earth that is empty and unformed, yet God’s Spirit is already present over the water. Everything else has a beginning in Him; He has no beginning Himself.
elements.mainPoint: God alone is eternal. He is the **Creator**, and everything else has its beginning in Him.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: Verse 2 says “the Spirit of God” was moving over the water. What might that add to the picture of who was present at creation?

elements.text: God speaks – and it is so
One of the most striking things about Genesis 1 is how God creates. There is no struggle and no effort. He speaks, and it is so.

elements.passageText: 3God said, “Let there be light.” And there was light! 4God saw that the light was good, so God separated the light from the darkness. 5God called the light “day” and the darkness “night.” There was evening, and there was morning, marking the first day.

elements.question: How does God bring light into existence, and what does that suggest about His power?
elements.questionHint: Look at what comes between “God said” and “there was light”.
elements.sampleAnswer: God creates by speaking: He says “Let there be light”, and light exists. Nothing comes between His word and the result, with no struggle, no delay and no resistance. That shows His word carries complete authority: what He says, happens. He then separates the light from the darkness and names them, ordering what He has made as well as making it.
elements.mainPoint: God creates by His **word alone**; what He says, happens.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: In verse 5 God names the light and the darkness. What might naming suggest about God’s relationship to what He has made?

9God said, “Let the water under the sky be gathered to one place and let dry ground appear.” It was so. 10God called the dry ground “land” and the gathered waters he called “seas.” God saw that it was good.

elements.question: In verses 6–10, who is active and who is acted upon? What does that show about the difference between God and what He makes?
elements.questionHint:
List the verbs.
What does God do?
What do the water, sky and land do?
elements.sampleAnswer: God speaks, makes, separates, gathers and names. The water, sky and land are shaped and placed by His word; they do not act on their own or resist Him. God stands over them as their Maker, not as one more part of the world. The passage gives us a Creator who is distinct from His creation and in charge of it.
elements.mainPoint: God is **distinct from creation** and sovereign over it: He shapes it by His word and is not part of it.

elements.text: Creation is ordered and good

As God continues to create, a rhythm emerges: God speaks, something comes into being, and, repeatedly, God sees that it is good. That tells us something about God’s character, and about the world He made.

elements.question: Read through verses 3–25. Which phrases and steps repeat as God creates?
elements.questionHint: Compare the opening and closing sentences of two or three of the days.
elements.sampleAnswer: Most stages follow the same pattern: God speaks (“God said…”), it happens (“It was so”), He names, makes or blesses what He has made, and He sees that it is good. Many of the days close with “there was evening, and there was morning”. The repetition shows careful, ordered work rather than chaos or chance, and it is God’s word that drives each step.
elements.mainPoint: Creation is **ordered and purposeful**: God works step by step by His word, and the repeated pattern points to design, not chance.

elements.question: What does the repeated verdict “God saw that it was good” tell us about God and about creation?
elements.questionHint: Notice who is making the judgement each time.
elements.sampleAnswer: The verdict is God’s own: He looks at what He has made and declares it good. That tells us He takes delight in His creation and is neither indifferent to it nor embarrassed by it. It also means the physical world is not evil or something to escape; it was made good and matters to God. Because the verdict is repeated at each stage, goodness belongs to the design from the start.
elements.mainPoint: God Himself calls creation **good**: the physical world is not evil or accidental, but made well and valued by its Maker.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: If the world is “good” in God’s own judgement, how might that shape the way you think about something as ordinary as a tree, a meal or the sky?

elements.text: The high point of creation

So far God has made light, sky, seas and land, plants and animals. When He comes to humanity, the language changes: “Let us make humankind in our image, after our likeness.” (Genesis 1:26, NET) No other creature is described like this. To be made in God’s image is to be made to represent Him on earth and to live in relationship with Him.

elements.passageText:
26Then God said, “Let us make humankind in our image, after our likeness, so they may rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of the air, over the cattle, and over all the earth, and over all the creatures that move on the earth.”

27God created humankind in his own image,
in the image of God he created them,
male and female he created them.

28God blessed them and said to them, “Be fruitful and multiply! Fill the earth and subdue it! Rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of the air and every creature that moves on the ground.”

elements.question: How does verse 26 introduce the creation of humanity differently from the rest of creation?
elements.questionHint: Compare “Let there be…” earlier in the chapter with how verse 26 begins.
elements.sampleAnswer: Earlier God commands things into being with “Let there be…”. Here He says “Let us make humankind”, as if deliberating, and speaks of making them in His own image and likeness. Nothing else in the chapter is described this way. Humanity is also given rule over the other creatures, so these verses set people apart within creation.
elements.mainPoint: Humanity is distinct within creation: made in **God’s image** and given a role of rule under Him.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: “Let us make” hints at plurality within God. What might it mean to be made in the image of a God for whom relationship is fundamental?

elements.question: Verse 27 says God created humankind “in his own image”. From what these verses say, what does it mean to be made in God’s image?
elements.questionHint: Look at what verses 26–28 connect with the image: the rule in verse 26 and “male and female” in verse 27.
elements.sampleAnswer: The passage does not tie the image to one ability, such as reason; it speaks of humanity as a whole. We are made to represent God on earth, ruling creation on His behalf, and to live in relationship, since verse 27 speaks of them as male and female together. It gives every human being dignity, because it is who we are, not something we earn.
elements.mainPoint: As the book puts it, humanity **is** God’s image. It is not one faculty such as reason but all of us, made to represent God on earth and to live in relationship.

elements.text: A life with purpose

God does not only make humans; He gives them a role: “Fill the earth and subdue it!” (Genesis 1:28, NET) That is a commission, not a burden. Human beings are placed in creation with something to do and something to care for.

elements.question: What does God commission humanity to do in verse 28?
elements.questionHint:
Count the commands in verse 28.
Note what each is about.
elements.sampleAnswer: God tells them to be fruitful, to multiply and to fill the earth, and to subdue it and rule over the fish, the birds and every living creature. There are two sides to the commission: filling the earth with people, and exercising authority over the rest of creation. It is given within a blessing, so it is a gift as well as a task. Because it is given to those made in God’s image, their rule is delegated by Him, not independent of Him.
elements.mainPoint: God’s blessing includes a **commission**: to fill the earth and to rule over creation as His representatives, with care rather than domination.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: Verse 28 uses strong words: “subdue” and “rule”. How would you expect a ruler made in the image of a good Creator to exercise that rule?

elements.passageText:
28God blessed them and said to them, “Be fruitful and multiply! Fill the earth and subdue it! Rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of the air and every creature that moves on the ground.” 29Then God said, “I now give you every seed-bearing plant on the face of the entire earth and every tree that has fruit with seed in it. They will be yours for food. 30And to all the animals of the earth, and to every bird of the air, and to all the creatures that move on the ground—everything that has living breath in it—I give every green plant for food.” It was so.

31God saw all that he had made—and it was very good! There was evening, and there was morning, the sixth day.

elements.question: In verses 29–31, what does God provide for what He has made, and how does He sum up His work?
elements.questionHint:
Look at what God gives in verses 29–30.
Look at His verdict in verse 31.
elements.sampleAnswer: God gives plants that yield seed and trees that bear fruit as food for humans, and green plants as food for the animals and birds. Creation comes with provision built in, which shows His generosity. At the end He looks at all that He has made and calls it very good. The story of humanity begins with provision and goodness, not scarcity or struggle.
elements.mainPoint: Creation is a **gift**: God generously provides for what He has made and calls all of it “very good”.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: If human life begins with God’s deliberate act, blessing and commission, what difference might that make to the question “Does my life have any meaning?”

elements.text: God ceases from His work

On the seventh day God ceases from His work. Not because He is tired (the one who spoke the universe into being does not need a break) but because the work is complete. He steps back, and He blesses the day and sets it apart.

elements.passageText: 1The heavens and the earth were completed with everything that was in them. 2By the seventh day God finished the work that he had been doing, and he ceased on the seventh day all the work that he had been doing. 3God blessed the seventh day and made it holy because on it he ceased all the work that he had been doing in creation.

elements.question: What does Genesis 2:1–3 say God did on the seventh day, and what does it say about the day itself?
elements.questionHint:
Notice the verbs.
What did God do on the seventh day?
What did He do to the day?
elements.sampleAnswer: God finished His work and ceased from it on the seventh day. This is not rest after exhaustion; it is the stopping that comes when the work is complete. He then blessed the seventh day and made it holy, setting it apart from the other days. The passage presents this pause as part of creation’s design from the start.
elements.mainPoint: God’s work is **complete**, and He sets apart the seventh day by blessing it and making it holy.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: The seventh day is blessed and made holy before humanity has done a day’s work. What might that suggest about how work and rest belong together in the life God designed?

elements.text: Reflection Questions

elements.question: Which gift of creation (a meal, a view, a night’s sleep) can I receive this week with thanks to the Creator?
Where does my sense of worth rest at the moment: what I do, who I am with, or what God has made me?
Where do I live as if I were more than a creature, refusing limits, rest or help?

elements.text: Prayer Focus

• Thank God for creating the world, and for creating you
  • Praise Him for His power and the goodness of what He has made
  • Ask Him to help you live with a sense of purpose
  • Thank Him that your life is not an accident
‘God, thank You for creating me and giving my life purpose. Help me to know You more, and to live the way You designed me to live.’
This Week

Choose at least one:
  • Spend 10-15 minutes outside observing creation – and reflect on what it tells you about God
  • Write down three things creation shows you about His character
  • Begin each day this week by acknowledging: ‘God, You made this day and You made me’
  • Receive one gift of creation this week (a meal, a view) with thanks to the Creator
  • Treat one person with intentional dignity, remembering that they too are made in God’s image

Genesis 1 gives us the wide-angle view: God speaks, the world comes into being, and everything is good. But Genesis 2 slows down. It zooms in on a single human being — how he is made, where he is placed, what he is given, and what he needs. The God of Genesis 1 who commanded light into existence is the same God who, in Genesis 2, gets His hands dirty.

4This is the account of the heavens and the earth when they were created—when the Lord God made the earth and heavens.

5Now no shrub of the field had yet grown on the earth, and no plant of the field had yet sprouted, for the Lord God had not caused it to rain on the earth, and there was no man to cultivate the ground. 6Springs would well up from the earth and water the whole surface of the ground. 7The Lord God formed the man from the soil of the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living being.

elements.question: How does verse 7 describe the way God makes the man, and what gives him life?
elements.questionHint: Look at the two things the Lord God does in verse 7.
elements.sampleAnswer: The Lord God “formed” the man from the soil of the ground, like a potter shaping clay. Then He breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living being. His body comes from the earth, but his life comes directly from God. The words show a God who is close, personal and hands-on.
elements.mainPoint: Humanity is **earthy and God-breathed**: formed from the ground like the rest of creation, yet given life by God’s own close, personal act.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: Genesis 1 shows God speaking creation into being; here He forms a man and breathes into him. What does each picture add to your understanding of God?

elements.text: Placed and given work

God doesn’t simply create the man and leave him to find his own way. He places him somewhere specific and gives him something to do.

“The Lord God took the man and placed him in the orchard in Eden to care for it and to maintain it.” (Genesis 2:15, NET)

This is important. Work appears here before the fall — before anything goes wrong. It is not a punishment for sin. It is part of what it means to be human, part of God’s good design.

elements.passageText:
8The Lord God planted an orchard in the east, in Eden; and there he placed the man he had formed. 9The Lord God made all kinds of trees grow from the soil, every tree that was pleasing to look at and good for food. 10Now a river flows from Eden to water the orchard, and from there it divides into four headstreams. 11The name of the first is Pishon; it runs through the entire land of Havilah, where there is gold. 12(The gold of that land is pure; pearls and lapis lazuli are also there.) 13The name of the second river is Gihon; it runs through the entire land of Cush. 14The name of the third river is Tigris; it runs along the east side of Assyria. 15The Lord God took the man and placed him in the orchard in Eden to care for it and to maintain it.

elements.question: What does God provide for the man in the garden, and what does He ask him to do (verse 15)?
elements.questionHint: Look at the two verbs God uses of the man’s task in verse 15.
elements.sampleAnswer: God plants a garden full of trees that are good to look at and good for food, with water to sustain it, and places the man there. Then He gives him a task: “to care for it and to maintain it”. The man is not just a guest enjoying the garden; he has a responsibility to look after it. This comes before anything goes wrong in the story, so work is part of the good life God designed.
elements.mainPoint: Work is part of God’s **good design**: the man is given a garden to care for before anything has gone wrong.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: Work appears here before sin enters. What might that suggest about the longing many people feel to do something meaningful, and about the pain of work that is frustrating or missing?

elements.text: Freedom and one boundary

What God gives is remarkable in its generosity. Every tree, every fruit — except one. The restriction is narrow; the freedom is vast. But the command also carries weight: this is the point at which trust becomes possible. You can only really choose to trust someone when there is something you could choose differently.

elements.passageText: 16Then the Lord God commanded the man, “You may freely eat fruit from every tree of the orchard, 17but you must not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, for when you eat from it you will surely die.”

elements.question: What does God allow, and what does He forbid, in verses 16–17?
elements.questionHint:
Notice the word “freely”.
Notice how many trees fall into each group.
elements.sampleAnswer: God allows the man to eat freely from every tree of the orchard. He forbids just one, the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, and warns that eating from it will bring death. The permission is wide and generous, and the restriction is narrow and specific. God is not stingy; He gives abundantly and sets one limit.
elements.mainPoint: God’s command is **generous with one boundary**: freedom to eat from every tree but one.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: A boundary gives trust something to do: the man can take God at His word or go his own way. What might that show about the kind of relationship God wants?

elements.text: People sometimes ask, ‘Why couldn’t God have made the garden without that tree in it?’ But the point isn’t really about the tree. The tree represents a bigger issue: Who is in control? It takes an abstract choice — will humanity acknowledge that God is God, or will they try to fill the role of being god-for-themselves — and makes it concrete. Will they trust what God says about this tree — or will they decide that they know better.
‘It is not good’

Throughout Genesis 1, the refrain has been ‘it was good.’ Now, for the first time, something is described differently.

“It is not good for the man to be alone.” (Genesis 2:18, NET)

This is striking. In the middle of a brilliant world — a world without sin — God identifies a gap. Humans are not designed to be solitary. The need for relationship — for genuine connection with others — is not a weakness or a product of the fall. It is part of how we were made.

elements.passageText: 18The Lord God said, “It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make a companion for him who corresponds to him.” 19The Lord God formed out of the ground every living animal of the field and every bird of the air. He brought them to the man to see what he would name them, and whatever the man called each living creature, that was its name. 20So the man named all the animals, the birds of the air, and the living creatures of the field, but for Adam no companion who corresponded to him was found.

elements.question: What does God call “not good” in verse 18, and what does He decide to do about it?
elements.questionHint:
Notice what the Lord God says is “not good”.
Notice what kind of companion He plans.
elements.sampleAnswer: God says it is not good for the man to be alone. This is the first time anything in the story is called “not good”, in a world He has just made good. God says He will make a companion for him who corresponds to him, someone who truly matches him. So the need for relationship is not a weakness; it is part of how humans were made.
elements.mainPoint: Even in a good world, being alone is **”not good”**: we are made for relationship, and God Himself sees the need.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: The first thing called “not good” is being alone. What might that suggest about being made in the image of a God who is Himself in relationship?

elements.question: What does the man do with the animals in verses 19–20, and what is the result?
elements.questionHint:
Look at what God brings to the man.
Look at what the man does.
Look at what is not found.
elements.sampleAnswer: God brings the animals to the man to see what he will name them, and he names them all. This shows the man exercising a role over them. But among all of them, no companion who corresponded to him was found. The animals are good, but they cannot meet this need; humans are different from them and made for one another.
elements.mainPoint: The man names the animals, a sign of his **role under God**, but no creature corresponds to him: humans are distinct, and made for each other.

elements.text: God provides

God’s response to the man’s aloneness is not to simply instruct him to cope. He acts. He provides. The creation of the woman is an act of generosity — God addresses a real need in a specific and personal way.

elements.passageText:
21So the Lord God caused the man to fall into a deep sleep, and while he was asleep, he took part of the man’s side and closed up the place with flesh. 22Then the Lord God made a woman from the part he had taken out of the man, and he brought her to the man. 23Then the man said,

“This one at last is bone of my bones
and flesh of my flesh;
this one will be called ‘woman,’
for she was taken out of man.”

24That is why a man leaves his father and mother and unites with his wife, and they become one family.

elements.question: How does the man respond when he sees the woman (verse 23), and what does that show about how she was made?
elements.questionHint: Look at “at last” and “bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh”.
elements.sampleAnswer: The man responds with delight and recognition: “This one at last”. He says she is bone of his bones and flesh of his flesh, because she was taken out of man. She shares his nature and is his equal in worth, and she is also distinct from him. God Himself provided her, so the picture is one of glad belonging.
elements.mainPoint: The woman is the **companion the man needed**: made from the man, sharing his nature, and received with delight.

elements.question: What does verse 24 say a man does, and what do the couple become?
elements.questionHint: Look at the three things verse 24 says about the man and his wife.
elements.sampleAnswer: A man leaves his father and mother and unites with his wife, and the two become one family. The verse describes a change of loyalty: the first family is left, and a new one is formed. The word “unites” suggests a firm, lasting bond. God’s design for marriage is therefore a committed union, not a casual arrangement.
elements.mainPoint: God’s design for marriage is **leaving, joining and becoming one**: a new family formed in lasting commitment.

elements.text: Marriage is the primary context here, but the broader truth runs wider: we are made for deep, real, meaningful connection with others — and God takes that seriously.
No shame

Genesis 2 ends with a single verse that carries enormous weight: “The man and his wife were both naked, but they were not ashamed.” (Genesis 2:25, NET) There is no hiding, no performance, no fear of being truly known. This is what life was designed to look like — complete openness between people, and between people and God.

It won’t last. But it’s worth pausing to notice what was lost.

elements.passageText: 25The man and his wife were both naked, but they were not ashamed.

elements.question: What does verse 25 say about how the man and woman felt about being unclothed, and what does that suggest about their relationship?
elements.questionHint:
Notice the two parts of the verse.
Notice what they were.
Notice what they were not.
elements.sampleAnswer: They were both naked, but they were not ashamed. There was nothing to hide and no fear of being fully known. This suggests a relationship of complete openness, trust and security, where being seen brought joy rather than exposure. There was no need to perform or protect themselves.
elements.mainPoint: In the original design, being **fully known** brought joy, not shame: nothing to hide and nothing to fear.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: Shame and self-protection mark many relationships today. What does this verse suggest was the design, and what might have changed? (Genesis 3 begins to answer.)

elements.text: Reflection Questions

elements.question: Which of my strengths do I treat as my own achievement rather than a gift? What would thanksgiving for one of them look like this week?
Do I experience God as personal and close, or more distant? Why?
Which relationships in my life need more attention or investment right now?

  • Thank Him for the relationships in your life

‘God, thank You for knowing me and creating me with purpose. Help me to grow in my relationship with You and with others.’

chapters.chapterTitle: The Fall — Sin Enters the World

elements.text:
The world of Genesis 2 ends with a man and woman who are naked and not ashamed. What follows in Genesis 3 is one of the most important chapters in the entire Bible, because it explains something we all know to be true from experience: the world as we find it is not the world as it was meant to be. Something went wrong. Genesis 3 tells us what, and how, and with what consequences.

It also — quietly, almost in passing — tells us that God has not given up.

elements.question: It’s worth reading the whole passage before you begin...
elements.answer:
1Now the serpent was shrewder than any of the wild animals that the Lord God had made. He said to the woman, “Is it really true that God said, ‘You must not eat from any tree of the orchard’?” 2The woman said to the serpent, “We may eat of the fruit from the trees of the orchard; 3but concerning the fruit of the tree that is in the middle of the orchard God said, ‘You must not eat from it, and you must not touch it, or else you will die.’” 4The serpent said to the woman, “Surely you will not die, 5for God knows that when you eat from it your eyes will open and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.”

6When the woman saw that the tree produced fruit that was good for food, was attractive to the eye, and was desirable for making one wise, she took some of its fruit and ate it. She also gave some of it to her husband who was with her, and he ate it. 7Then the eyes of both of them opened, and they knew they were naked; so they sewed fig leaves together and made coverings for themselves.

8Then the man and his wife heard the sound of the Lord God moving about in the orchard at the breezy time of the day, and they hid from the Lord God among the trees of the orchard. 9But the Lord God called to the man and said to him, “Where are you?” 10The man replied, “I heard you moving about in the orchard, and I was afraid because I was naked, so I hid.” 11And the Lord God said, “Who told you that you were naked? Did you eat from the tree that I commanded you not to eat from?” 12The man said, “The woman whom you gave me, she gave me some fruit from the tree and I ate it.” 13So the Lord God said to the woman, “What is this you have done?” And the woman replied, “The serpent tricked me, and I ate.”

14The Lord God said to the serpent,

“Because you have done this,
cursed are you above all the cattle
and all the living creatures of the field!
On your belly you will crawl
and dust you will eat all the days of your life.
15And I will put hostility between you and the woman
and between your offspring and her offspring;
he will strike your head,
and you will strike his heel.”

16To the woman he said,

“I will greatly increase your labor pains;
with pain you will give birth to children.
You will want to control your husband,
but he will dominate you.”

17But to Adam he said,

“Because you obeyed your wife
and ate from the tree about which I commanded you,
‘You must not eat from it,’
the ground is cursed because of you;
in painful toil you will eat of it all the days of your life.
18It will produce thorns and thistles for you,
but you will eat the grain of the field.
19By the sweat of your brow you will eat food
until you return to the ground,
for out of it you were taken;
for you are dust, and to dust you will return.”

20The man named his wife Eve, because she was the mother of all the living. 21The Lord God made garments from skin for Adam and his wife, and clothed them. 22And the Lord God said, “Now that the man has become like one of us, knowing good and evil, he must not be allowed to stretch out his hand and take also from the tree of life and eat, and live forever.” 23So the Lord God expelled him from the orchard in Eden to cultivate the ground from which he had been taken. 24When he drove the man out, he placed on the eastern side of the orchard in Eden angelic sentries who used the flame of a whirling sword to guard the way to the tree of life.

NET – see context ↗

elements.text: A question designed to unsettle

The serpent doesn’t begin with an outright lie. He begins with a question.

“Is it really true that God said…?” (Genesis 3:1, NET)

It’s a small move, but a precise one. The question doesn’t deny what God said — it just introduces a little uncertainty, a little space for doubt. Is God really as generous as He seemed? Is the boundary really as reasonable as it appeared?

elements.passageText:
16Then the Lord God commanded the man, “You may freely eat fruit from every tree of the orchard, 17but you must not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, for when you eat from it you will surely die.”

3:1Now the serpent was shrewder than any of the wild animals that the Lord God had made. He said to the woman, “Is it really true that God said, ‘You must not eat from any tree of the orchard’?” 3:2The woman said to the serpent, “We may eat of the fruit from the trees of the orchard; 3:3but concerning the fruit of the tree that is in the middle of the orchard God said, ‘You must not eat from it, and you must not touch it, or else you will die.’” 3:4The serpent said to the woman, “Surely you will not die, 3:5for God knows that when you eat from it your eyes will open and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.”

elements.question: How does the serpent’s question in verse 1 differ from what God actually said in 2:16–17?
elements.questionHint: Compare “any tree of the orchard” in 3:1 with “every tree… but” in 2:16–17.
elements.sampleAnswer: God had said the man could eat freely from every tree except one. The serpent asks whether God said they must not eat from any tree, which exaggerates the command and makes God sound harsh and stingy. He does not deny what God said; he begins with a question that plants doubt about whether God can be trusted. A small distortion opens the door for a bigger lie.
elements.mainPoint: The serpent begins not with a denial but with a **distortion**: he makes God’s generous command sound like a harsh ban.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: Doubts about whether God’s commands are good for us still arise today. Where do you hear echoes of the serpent’s question?

elements.question: What does the serpent claim in verses 4–5 about death and about God’s motives?
elements.questionHint:
Notice what the serpent says God “knows”.
Notice what he says will happen.
elements.sampleAnswer: The serpent flatly contradicts God’s warning: “Surely you will not die”. He then suggests that God is holding something back: God knows that when they eat, their eyes will open and they will be like God. That paints God as selfish and untrustworthy, keeping them from something good because He does not want rivals. Disobedience begins to look like gaining something rather than losing everything.
keyTerms: like god|become god|equal|know good and evil
elements.mainPoint: The serpent paints God as a **rival who is holding something back**, so that disobedience looks like a gain.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: By the end of the chapter their eyes are opened and they know good and evil (3:7, 22). In what sense was the serpent right, and in what sense terribly wrong?

elements.question: What does Eve add to God’s command when she repeats it in verse 3?
elements.questionHint: Compare “you must not touch it” in 3:3 with what God said in 2:16–17.
elements.sampleAnswer: Eve correctly says they may eat from the trees and that the tree in the middle is forbidden. But she adds that they must not touch it, which God did not say. The text does not tell us whether she added this herself or heard it from Adam. Either way, God’s word is already being reshaped in her mind before she is tempted.
keyTerms: tree in the middle|forbidden tree|middle of the garden
elements.mainPoint: Eve’s reply shows the first cracks: she **adds to** what God said, so His command is already being reshaped.

elements.text: The decision

The temptation works not by force but by desire. The woman looks at the fruit and sees that it is good to eat, pleasing to the eye, desirable for gaining wisdom. Each of those things is appealing in itself. The problem is not desire — the problem is taking what God has withheld.

elements.passageText: 6When the woman saw that the tree produced fruit that was good for food, was attractive to the eye, and was desirable for making one wise, she took some of its fruit and ate it. She also gave some of it to her husband who was with her, and he ate it.

elements.question: What reasons does verse 6 give for the woman taking the fruit, and what does she do next?
elements.questionHint: Count the three descriptions of the tree, then notice who else is mentioned.
elements.sampleAnswer: She sees that the tree is good for food, attractive to the eye and desirable for making one wise. Each of these is something good in itself. She takes the fruit and eats it, then gives some to her husband, who was with her, and he eats. The problem is not that she wanted good things but that she took them by deciding for herself what God had withheld.
elements.mainPoint: Temptation works through **real and appealing goods** offered by a route God has forbidden: she takes what she wants and decides for herself.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: The fruit offered food, beauty and wisdom, all good things. What does that suggest about how temptation usually works, and where might it show up for you?

elements.text: The problem here is not just Eve and Adam breaking the rules (although they do do that). The problem is that they want to become the ones who make the rules. In reaching out to take the fruit, they are reaching out to take God’s place. They want to be the rule-makers in their own lives. And very often we are just like them.
Everything changes

The moment they eat, something shifts. They expected to gain; instead, they feel exposed. The eyes that were opened don’t see wisdom — they see their own nakedness, and they are ashamed.

Then they hear God approaching, and they hide. This is new. Nothing in Genesis 2 suggested any reason to hide from God. Now, instinctively, that is exactly what they do.

elements.passageText:
7Then the eyes of both of them opened, and they knew they were naked; so they sewed fig leaves together and made coverings for themselves.

8Then the man and his wife heard the sound of the Lord God moving about in the orchard at the breezy time of the day, and they hid from the Lord God among the trees of the orchard. 9But the Lord God called to the man and said to him, “Where are you?” 10The man replied, “I heard you moving about in the orchard, and I was afraid because I was naked, so I hid.”

elements.question: In 2:25 the couple were “naked, but they were not ashamed”. What changes in verses 7–10?
elements.questionHint:
Look at what they know.
Look at what they make.
Look at what they do when they hear the Lord God.
elements.sampleAnswer: Their eyes are opened and they know they are naked, so shame has arrived. They sew fig leaves together to cover themselves, which is self-protection in place of openness. When they hear the Lord God moving in the orchard, they hide from Him, and the man says he was afraid. Shame, concealment and fear replace the ease they had before.
elements.mainPoint: Sin brings **shame, hiding and fear**: openness with each other and with God gives way to cover-up.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: They ate hoping to gain something, yet their first experience is exposure, not triumph. Why might that be?

elements.text: Blame and broken relationships

When God confronts them, neither the man nor the woman takes responsibility. The man blames the woman — and, subtly, blames God for giving her to him. The woman blames the serpent. Sin has not only broken their relationship with God; it has immediately begun to fracture their relationship with each other.

elements.passageText: 11And the Lord God said, “Who told you that you were naked? Did you eat from the tree that I commanded you not to eat from?” 12The man said, “The woman whom you gave me, she gave me some fruit from the tree and I ate it.” 13So the Lord God said to the woman, “What is this you have done?” And the woman replied, “The serpent tricked me, and I ate.”

elements.question: How do the man and the woman each answer when God questions them?
elements.questionHint: Look at what each adds after admitting that they ate.
elements.sampleAnswer: Both admit they ate, but both shift the blame. The man blames the woman, and in doing so implicitly blames God, who gave her to him. The woman blames the serpent. Neither takes full responsibility, so sin has already begun to fracture their relationship with each other as well as with God.
elements.mainPoint: Sin immediately fractures relationships: each **shifts the blame** and no one takes responsibility.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: Avoiding responsibility is a very common response when we are caught. What do we risk by owning up, and what do we protect by deflecting?

elements.text: The consequences

God’s response is not an explosion of anger, but a careful and serious declaration of consequences. Pain, struggle, broken relationships, hard work, and — finally — death. The world will continue to exist, but the ease and wholeness of Genesis 2 is gone. These consequences are layered on top of the blessings of creation; they do not cancel them.

elements.passageText:
14The Lord God said to the serpent,

“Because you have done this,
cursed are you above all the cattle
and all the living creatures of the field!
On your belly you will crawl
and dust you will eat all the days of your life.
15And I will put hostility between you and the woman
and between your offspring and her offspring;
he will strike your head,
and you will strike his heel.”

16To the woman he said,

“I will greatly increase your labor pains;
with pain you will give birth to children.
You will want to control your husband,
but he will dominate you.”

17But to Adam he said,

“Because you obeyed your wife
and ate from the tree about which I commanded you,
‘You must not eat from it,’
the ground is cursed because of you;
in painful toil you will eat of it all the days of your life.
18It will produce thorns and thistles for you,
but you will eat the grain of the field.
19By the sweat of your brow you will eat food
until you return to the ground,
for out of it you were taken;
for you are dust, and to dust you will return.”

elements.question: What does God say will change for the serpent, the woman and the man?
elements.questionHint: Take each in turn: the serpent (verses 14–15), the woman (verse 16), the man (verses 17–19).
elements.sampleAnswer: The serpent is cursed and will be at enmity with the woman and her offspring. The woman will have greatly increased pain in childbirth, and there will be conflict in her relationship with her husband. For the man, the ground is cursed: his work will be painful toil among thorns and thistles. And finally both will return to the dust, so death is the end of every life. Good things remain, but everything is now shadowed by pain, struggle and mortality.
elements.mainPoint: The consequences reach **every area of life**: childbirth, relationships, work and finally death. They are layered on top of creation’s blessings, not a cancellation of them.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: Which of these effects can you see in the world around you today?

elements.text: A promise hidden in judgement
In the middle of God’s words to the serpent, something unexpected appears: a promise. It is only one verse, so read it slowly. Tap the reference on the next question to see it.

elements.passageText:
15And I will put hostility between you and the woman
and between your offspring and her offspring;
he will strike your head,
and you will strike his heel.”

elements.text: This is the first hint in the Bible that evil will not have the final word. God is already pointing toward a rescue. The one who will defeat the serpent has not yet come — but the promise is made. Even here, in the moment of judgement, God does not abandon humanity.

elements.question: What does God promise in verse 15, and how does the conflict end?
elements.questionHint: Notice the two parts of the conflict: whose head is struck, and whose heel.
elements.sampleAnswer: God will put hostility between the serpent and the woman, and between their offspring. One of the woman’s offspring will strike the serpent’s head, while the serpent will strike his heel. A blow to the head is decisive; a blow to the heel wounds but does not finish. So the promise is of eventual victory over the serpent, at a cost. The verse does not say who this offspring will be, and it comes in the middle of judgement.
elements.mainPoint: Even as God pronounces judgement, He promises a **coming Serpent-crusher**: evil will not have the last word.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: The promise comes while God is still speaking judgement, before anyone has repented. What does the timing suggest about His commitment to humanity?

elements.text: Covered and sent out

Two final acts close the chapter. God makes garments for the man and woman and clothes them — taking over from their own inadequate attempt to cover themselves. And then He sends them out of the garden. Both acts matter. The covering suggests that God takes their shame seriously and addresses it Himself. The sending away, painful as it is, contains a mercy: they are protected from living forever in their fallen state.

elements.passageText: 21The Lord God made garments from skin for Adam and his wife, and clothed them.

elements.question: What does God do for Adam and Eve in verse 21, and how does that compare with what they did for themselves in verse 7?
elements.questionHint:
Compare “fig leaves” in verse 7 with “garments from skin” here.
Notice who makes each.
elements.sampleAnswer: In verse 7 the couple sew fig leaves together to cover themselves. In verse 21 the Lord God Himself makes garments from skin and clothes them. Their own attempt to deal with their shame is replaced by something God provides. This comes right after the curses and just before the expulsion, so even in judgement God is still caring for them.
elements.mainPoint: Before He sends them out, **God clothes them Himself**: judgement and mercy together.

elements.passageText: 22And the Lord God said, “Now that the man has become like one of us, knowing good and evil, he must not be allowed to stretch out his hand and take also from the tree of life and eat, and live forever.” 23So the Lord God expelled him from the orchard in Eden to cultivate the ground from which he had been taken. 24When he drove the man out, he placed on the eastern side of the orchard in Eden angelic sentries who used the flame of a whirling sword to guard the way to the tree of life.

elements.question: Why does God send the man out of the garden, and in what sense might that also be an act of mercy?
elements.questionHint:
Read God’s reasoning in verse 22.
What must not be allowed to happen?
elements.sampleAnswer: Now that the man knows good and evil, God will not let him reach out to the tree of life and live forever. So He expels him and posts sentries with a flaming sword to guard the way. This is judgement: they lose the garden and the closeness that came with it. Yet it is also merciful, because it stops humanity living on for ever in its fallen condition, and it leaves room for the rescue that verse 15 has begun to promise.
elements.mainPoint: The exile is **both judgement and mercy**: sin must be banished, and God will not let humanity live forever in its fallen state.

elements.text: Reflection Questions

elements.question: When I fail, do I return to God in repentance, or do I hide, make excuses or reach for a hollow self-righteousness?
What good thing have I made into a “god-thing”? What gives me meaning, purpose and security?
Where am I most likely to “sin more than I know”? Who could tell me honestly?

elements.text: Prayer Focus

• Confess personal sin honestly to God
  • Ask for help to resist temptation
  • Thank God that He does not give up on us
  • Thank Him for His plan to rescue and restore

‘God, I see how sin affects my life. Please forgive me, and help me to trust You and follow You.’
This Week

Choose at least one:
  • Identify one area where you are often tempted, and take one practical step to address it
  • When tempted this week, pause and ask: ‘Is this trusting God — or not?’
  • Be honest with God about a struggle you have been keeping hidden
  • Reflect on the promise of Genesis 3:15 — that God has a rescue plan — and let that shape how you pray

One of the uncomfortable truths about sin is that it doesn’t stay still. Left unaddressed, it grows — in intensity, in reach, in the damage it causes. Genesis 3 showed us how sin entered the world through one act of disobedience. Genesis 4 shows us what sin does next: it spreads into the first human family, and the results are devastating. By the end of the chapter it has spread beyond the family into the wider society.

elements.question: It’s worth reading the whole passage before you begin...
elements.answer:
1Now the man was intimate with his wife Eve, and she became pregnant and gave birth to Cain. Then she said, “I have created a man just as the Lord did!” 2Then she gave birth to his brother Abel. Abel took care of the flocks, while Cain cultivated the ground.

3At the designated time Cain brought some of the fruit of the ground for an offering to the Lord. 4But Abel brought some of the firstborn of his flock—even the fattest of them. And the Lord was pleased with Abel and his offering, 5but with Cain and his offering he was not pleased. So Cain became very angry, and his expression was downcast.

6Then the Lord said to Cain, “Why are you angry, and why is your expression downcast? 7Is it not true that if you do what is right, you will be fine? But if you do not do what is right, sin is crouching at the door. It desires to dominate you, but you must subdue it.”

8Cain said to his brother Abel, “Let’s go out to the field.” While they were in the field, Cain attacked his brother Abel and killed him.

9Then the Lord said to Cain, “Where is your brother Abel?” And he replied, “I don’t know! Am I my brother’s guardian?” 10But the Lord said, “What have you done? The voice of your brother’s blood is crying out to me from the ground! 11So now you are banished from the ground, which has opened its mouth to receive your brother’s blood from your hand. 12When you try to cultivate the ground it will no longer yield its best for you. I will be a homeless wanderer on the earth; whoever finds me will kill me!” 15But the Lord said to him, “All right then, if anyone kills Cain, Cain will be avenged seven times as much.” Then the Lord put a special mark on Cain so that no one who found him would strike him down. 16So Cain went out from the presence of the Lord and lived in the land of Nod, east of Eden.

elements.text: Two offerings
The story opens with two brothers bringing offerings to God. On the surface, they seem to be doing the same thing. But God responds to them very differently.

elements.passageText:
1Now the man was intimate with his wife Eve, and she became pregnant and gave birth to Cain. Then she said, “I have created a man just as the Lord did!” 2Then she gave birth to his brother Abel. Abel took care of the flocks, while Cain cultivated the ground.

3At the designated time Cain brought some of the fruit of the ground for an offering to the Lord. 4But Abel brought some of the firstborn of his flock—even the fattest of them. And the Lord was pleased with Abel and his offering, 5but with Cain and his offering he was not pleased. So Cain became very angry, and his expression was downcast.

elements.question: What does the narrator tell us about each brother’s offering and about how the Lord responded?
elements.questionHint: Compare the words used for each offering, then for the Lord’s response.
elements.sampleAnswer: Cain brought some of the fruit of the ground. Abel brought some of the firstborn of his flock, even the fattest of them. The Lord was pleased with Abel and his offering, but not with Cain and his. The passage does not say why, though it describes Abel’s offering in more detail. Cain’s response is to become very angry, with a downcast face.
elements.mainPoint: The Lord accepts one offering and not the other, and Cain’s response is **anger**.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: The passage does not say why the Lord favoured Abel’s offering. What clues does it give? Why might the narrator tell us so much about Abel’s offering and so little about Cain’s?

elements.text: The narrator tells us what each brother brought and how the Lord responded. He does not tell us why. Notice how much the text says about Abel’s offering, and how Cain reacts.
The warning

Cain’s response to God’s rejection is not repentance — it is anger. And God, rather than immediately judging him, does something remarkable: He speaks to Cain directly, and warns him.

This is one of the most vivid descriptions of sin in the whole Bible — not a mistake, not a moment of weakness, but something with agency, something that wants to dominate you.

elements.passageText: 6Then the Lord said to Cain, “Why are you angry, and why is your expression downcast? 7Is it not true that if you do what is right, you will be fine? But if you do not do what is right, sin is crouching at the door. It desires to dominate you, but you must subdue it.”

elements.question: How does the Lord speak to Cain in verses 6–7, and how does He describe sin?
elements.questionHint:
Notice the questions God asks.
Notice the verbs used of sin.
elements.sampleAnswer: The Lord speaks to Cain directly, with questions that invite him to look at himself. He says that if Cain does what is right he will be fine, but if not, sin is crouching at the door like a predator, desiring to dominate him. Yet Cain “must subdue it”: he is responsible, and he is able to resist. God warns him before anything worse happens.
elements.mainPoint: Sin is **active and dangerous**, crouching to dominate, but God warns Cain first and tells him that he must master it.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: God warns Cain before anything worse happens. What does that suggest about how God deals with sin?

elements.text: The first murder, and denial

Cain ignores the warning. He invites his brother into a field, and kills him.

What began in Genesis 3 as disobedience toward God has now become violence between people. This is the logic of unaddressed sin: it escalates.

God comes to Cain, just as He came to Adam and Eve. “Where is your brother Abel?” And Cain’s response — “Am I my brother’s guardian?” — reveals a hardness that goes beyond the sin itself. There is no regret. No remorse. Only deflection.

elements.passageText:
8Cain said to his brother Abel, “Let’s go out to the field.” While they were in the field, Cain attacked his brother Abel and killed him.

9Then the Lord said to Cain, “Where is your brother Abel?” And he replied, “I don’t know! Am I my brother’s guardian?” 10But the Lord said, “What have you done? The voice of your brother’s blood is crying out to me from the ground!

elements.question: How does Cain answer when God asks where Abel is, and what does God say in reply?
elements.questionHint: Look at what Cain says, then at what God says Abel’s blood is doing.
elements.sampleAnswer: Cain says “I don’t know!”, which is a lie, and then asks “Am I my brother’s guardian?”, refusing any responsibility. God answers with a question of His own: “What have you done?” He says the voice of Abel’s blood is crying out to Him from the ground. Cain hides behind a denial; God sees and hears what has happened to the victim.
elements.mainPoint: Cain **denies responsibility**, but God sees and hears: Abel’s blood cries out.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: In Genesis 3, Adam and Eve at least admitted that they ate. How does Cain’s answer differ, and what might that show about how sin hardens?

elements.text: Justice and mercy, together

Cain is judged — driven from the ground, cut off from productive work, a wanderer. But even here, God does not simply destroy him. He places a mark of protection on Cain, so that he will not be killed. Justice and mercy appear side by side — as they will again and again throughout Genesis.

elements.passageText:
11So now you are banished from the ground, which has opened its mouth to receive your brother’s blood from your hand. 12When you try to cultivate the ground it will no longer yield its best for you. You will be a homeless wanderer on the earth.”

13Then Cain said to the Lord, “My punishment is too great to endure! 14Look, you are driving me off the land today, and I must hide from your presence. I will be a homeless wanderer on the earth; whoever finds me will kill me!” 15But the Lord said to him, “All right then, if anyone kills Cain, Cain will be avenged seven times as much.” Then the Lord put a special mark on Cain so that no one who found him would strike him down. 16So Cain went out from the presence of the Lord and lived in the land of Nod, east of Eden.

elements.question: What are the consequences for Cain, and how does Cain describe them?
elements.questionHint:
Work through verses 11–14.
What does Cain lose?
elements.sampleAnswer: Cain is banished from the ground, and when he works it, it will no longer yield its best. He will be a homeless wanderer on the earth. Cain says his punishment is too great to endure, that he is driven from the land, and that he must hide from the Lord’s presence. His losses are his work, his place, and closeness to God.
elements.mainPoint: Sin’s consequences are **real and relational**: Cain loses the ground he worked, his home, and the Lord’s presence.

elements.question: How does God still show mercy to Cain, even though he is being judged?
elements.questionHint:
Look at what Cain fears in verse 14.
Look at what the Lord does about it in verse 15.
elements.sampleAnswer: Cain fears that anyone who finds him will kill him. The Lord promises that anyone who kills Cain will be avenged seven times over, and puts a special mark on him so that no one who finds him will strike him down. Cain has shown no sorrow for what he did, only fear for himself, yet God still protects him. Justice and mercy appear side by side.
elements.mainPoint: Justice and mercy go side by side: Cain is judged, yet God **protects** him.

elements.text: Sin accelerates

As the generations pass, the pattern grows darker. By the time we reach Lamech — Cain’s descendant — violence has become something to boast about.

“I have killed a man for wounding me… If Cain is to be avenged seven times as much, then Lamech seventy-seven times!” (Genesis 4:23–24, NET)

This is a man who has taken God’s mercy toward Cain and turned it into a licence for unrestrained revenge. What God extended as grace, Lamech wields as a weapon.

elements.passageText:
17Cain was intimate with his wife, and she became pregnant and gave birth to Enoch. Cain was building a city, and he named the city after his son Enoch. 18To Enoch was born Irad, and Irad was the father of Mehujael. Mehujael was the father of Methushael, and Methushael was the father of Lamech.

19Lamech took two wives for himself; the name of the first was Adah, and the name of the second was Zillah. 20Adah gave birth to Jabal; he was the first of those who live in tents and keep livestock. 21The name of his brother was Jubal; he was the first of all who play the harp and the flute. 22Now Zillah also gave birth to Tubal-Cain, who heated metal and shaped all kinds of tools made of bronze and iron. The sister of Tubal-Cain was Naamah.

23Lamech said to his wives,

“Adah and Zillah, listen to me!
You wives of Lamech, hear my words!
I have killed a man for wounding me,
a young man for hurting me.
24If Cain is to be avenged seven times as much,
then Lamech seventy-seven times!”

elements.question: What does Lamech say to his wives, and how does his attitude compare with Cain’s?
elements.questionHint:
Notice how Lamech speaks to his wives.
Notice what he says about vengeance and about Cain.
elements.sampleAnswer: Lamech openly tells his wives that he has killed a man for wounding him. He boasts that if Cain is avenged seven times, then he will be avenged seventy-seven times. Cain denied what he had done; Lamech is proud of it. He has also turned God’s protection of Cain into a licence for bigger vengeance. Violence has moved from a secret act to something to boast about.
elements.mainPoint: Sin **escalates**: from Cain’s secret murder to Lamech’s boast, violence becomes something to be proud of.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: Alongside the violence, verses 20–22 record tents, music and metalwork. What might that suggest about human culture after the Fall?

elements.text: A line of hope, and the sound of death

Yet even here, the chapter doesn’t end without hope. Another son is born — Seth — and, in the NET’s words, “people began to worship the Lord.” In the middle of a world descending into violence and pride, there are still those who turn toward God.

elements.passageText: 25And Adam was intimate with his wife again, and she gave birth to a son. She named him Seth, saying, “God has given me another child in place of Abel because Cain killed him.” 26And a son was also born to Seth, whom he named Enosh. At that time people began to worship the Lord.

elements.question: What signs of hope appear at the end of Genesis 4?
elements.questionHint:
Look at what Eve says about Seth.
Look at what people begin to do in verse 26.
elements.sampleAnswer: Eve gives birth to another son, Seth, and says God has given her another child in place of Abel. She sees him as God’s gift. Then a son is born to Seth, Enosh, and “at that time people began to worship the Lord”. Even as violence spreads, God provides a new line, and there are people who turn towards Him.
elements.mainPoint: Even as sin spreads, **God provides a new line**, and people begin to worship Him.

elements.text: Genesis 5 is a genealogy, easy to skip. It does two things worth noticing. It opens by looking back to the creation of humankind, and it repeats one phrase, entry after entry: “and then he died”. The two belong together.

elements.passageText:
1This is the record of the family line of Adam.

When God created humankind, he made them in the likeness of God. 2He created them male and female; when they were created, he blessed them and named them “humankind.”

3When Adam had lived 130 years he fathered a son in his own likeness, according to his image, and he named him Seth. 4The length of time Adam lived after he became the father of Seth was 800 years; during this time he had other sons and daughters. 5The entire lifetime of Adam was 930 years, and then he died.

8The entire lifetime of Seth was 912 years, and then he died.

11The entire lifetime of Enosh was 905 years, and then he died.

14The entire lifetime of Kenan was 910 years, and then he died.

17The entire lifetime of Mahalalel was 895 years, and then he died.

20The entire lifetime of Jared was 962 years, and then he died.

27The entire lifetime of Methuselah was 969 years, and then he died.

31The entire lifetime of Lamech was 777 years, and then he died.

elements.question: Genesis 5:1–3 looks back to the creation of humankind. What does it repeat from Genesis 1, and what is passed on from Adam to Seth?
elements.questionHint: Compare how God made humankind with how Adam fathered Seth.
elements.sampleAnswer: The passage recalls that when God created humankind He made them in His likeness, male and female, and blessed them. Then Adam fathers a son “in his own likeness, according to his image”, and names him Seth. The language of likeness and image is picked up again and carried to the next generation. Even after sin has entered, humanity is still described in terms of God’s likeness.
elements.mainPoint: Genesis 5 deliberately echoes Genesis 1: humanity is still described in terms of **God’s likeness**, even though sin has spread.

elements.question: What does the repeated phrase “and then he died” add to the story Genesis has been telling?
elements.questionHint: Look at how each of these entries ends, and remember God’s warning of death in Genesis 2:17.
elements.sampleAnswer: Each entry records a long life, and each ends with death. In Genesis 2:17 God had warned the man, “you will surely die”. Whether a man lived 900 years or fewer, none of them escaped. The refrain confirms that the consequence of Genesis 3 is real and universal, even as the human line continues.
elements.mainPoint: Death now **ends every life**, however long: the consequence God warned of is real.

Do I tend to deal with sin early, or let it linger? What makes the difference?
When I have done wrong, do I own it, or do I deflect, as Adam, Eve and Cain did?

By Genesis 6, the world has changed beyond recognition from the good creation of Genesis 1. Sin has spread across generations, grown more violent, more brazen, more widespread. The question that Genesis now forces is: what does a holy God do with a world that has become thoroughly corrupt? The flood is the answer — and it is deeply uncomfortable, and deeply important, in equal measure.

By the time it comes, the earth is filled with violence: what began with one couple, and spread to a family and then to a society, now fills the earth.

But the flood is not only a story about judgement. It is also a story about grace.

elements.text: A world shaped by sin

The description of humanity in Genesis 6 pulls no punches.

“Every inclination of the thoughts of their minds was only evil all the time.” (Genesis 6:5, NET)

This is not occasional wrongdoing. It is a thoroughgoing corruption — not just actions, but the inner life, the imagination, the will. And God’s response is not indifference: it is deeply personal.

elements.passageText: 5But the Lord saw that the wickedness of humankind had become great on the earth. Every inclination of the thoughts of their minds was only evil all the time. 6The Lord regretted that he had made humankind on the earth, and he was highly offended. 7So the Lord said, “I will wipe humankind, whom I have created, from the face of the earth—everything from humankind to animals, including creatures that move on the ground and birds of the air, for I regret that I have made them.”

elements.question: How does this passage describe humanity, and how does the Lord respond?
elements.questionHint: Notice the words “great”, “every”, “only” and “all the time”, then the Lord’s reaction in verses 6–7.
elements.sampleAnswer: The wickedness of humankind had become great on the earth. Every inclination of the thoughts of their minds was only evil all the time, which describes the inner life as well as actions. The Lord regretted that He had made humankind and was highly offended, and He resolved to wipe them out. God is not indifferent to sin; it provokes a real response.
elements.mainPoint: Sin has reached **every part of human life**, even the thoughts, and God does not shrug it off.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: What does it say about God that He is so deeply affected by sin, rather than indifferent to it?

elements.text: One man

In the middle of this description, a single word breaks the pattern: ‘But.’

“But Noah found favor in the sight of the Lord.” (Genesis 6:8, NET)

This is not about Noah being sinless or morally superior. It is about grace — God’s undeserved favour toward someone who walks with Him. The contrast with the surrounding world is stark.
