8But Noah found favor in the sight of the Lord.

9This is the account of Noah.

Noah was a godly man; he was blameless among his contemporaries. He walked with God. 10Noah had three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth.

elements.question: What does verse 8 say about Noah’s standing with God, and how does verse 9 describe him?
elements.questionHint: Notice the verb in verse 8 and the three phrases in verse 9.
elements.sampleAnswer: Noah “found favor in the sight of the Lord”. The text puts favour first, and only then describes him: a godly man, blameless among his contemporaries, who walked with God. He stands out in a world full of evil. He is not called sinless; he is described as someone whose whole life is lived close to God.
elements.mainPoint: Noah stands out because he **found favour** with God and walked with Him.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: Does the passage present Noah’s favour as something he earned, or something he received? What difference would it make?

elements.text: Faith expressed in obedience

God tells Noah to build an ark, with detailed instructions that would have required enormous time, effort, and commitment. And Noah obeys.

“Noah did all that God commanded him—he did indeed.” (Genesis 6:22, NET)

Faith and obedience are not separated here. Noah trusts God enough to act — in the face of what must have seemed absurd to those around him.

elements.passageText:
13So God said to Noah, “I have decided that all living creatures must die, for the earth is filled with violence because of them. Now I am about to destroy them and the earth. 14Make for yourself an ark of cypress wood. Make rooms in the ark, and cover it with pitch inside and out. 15This is how you should make it: The ark is to be 450 feet long, 75 feet wide, and 45 feet high. 16Make a roof for the ark and finish it, leaving 18 inches from the top. Put a door in the side of the ark, and make lower, middle, and upper decks. 17I am about to bring floodwaters on the earth to destroy from under the sky all the living creatures that have the breath of life in them. Everything that is on the earth will die, 18but I will confirm my covenant with you. You will enter the ark—you, your sons, your wife, and your sons’ wives with you. 19You must bring into the ark two of every kind of living creature from all flesh, male and female, to keep them alive with you. 20Of the birds after their kinds, and of the cattle after their kinds, and of every creeping thing of the ground after its kind, two of every kind will come to you so you can keep them alive. 21And you must take for yourself every kind of food that is eaten, and gather it together. It will be food for you and for them.”

22And Noah did all that God commanded him—he did indeed.

elements.question: What does God tell Noah He is going to do and why, and what does He ask Noah to do?
elements.questionHint:
Look at God’s reason in verse 13.
Look at His instructions from verse 14 on.
elements.sampleAnswer: God has decided that all living creatures must die, because the earth is filled with violence. He tells Noah to build an ark of cypress wood, 450 feet long, with rooms, pitch inside and out, a door and three decks. Noah is to bring pairs of every kind of living creature, along with food. God’s answer to the violence is judgement, together with a way of rescue.
elements.mainPoint: The earth is **filled with violence**, and God’s answer is judgement together with a way of rescue: an ark for Noah and the living creatures.

elements.question: What does verse 22 say about how Noah responds, and why might that have been hard?
elements.questionHint: Think about the scale of the task described in verses 14–21.
elements.sampleAnswer: Noah “did all that God commanded him”. That meant building a huge ark, with detailed specifications, and gathering food and animals, which would have taken great effort over a long time. He acts on God’s word, trusting a warning about something that has not yet happened in the story. His response shows faith expressed in obedience, not just belief.
elements.mainPoint: Noah **does everything God commands**: faith that acts on God’s word.

elements.text: The flood comes
The judgement, when it arrives, is total. The flood covers the earth. The world that had been shaped by sin is undone. This is deeply serious — and the text doesn’t soften it.

elements.passageText:
11In the six hundredth year of Noah’s life, in the second month, on the seventeenth day of the month—on that day all the fountains of the great deep burst open and the floodgates of the heavens were opened. 12And the rain fell on the earth forty days and forty nights.

13On that very day Noah entered the ark, accompanied by his sons Shem, Ham, and Japheth, along with his wife and his sons’ three wives. 14They entered, along with every living creature after its kind, every animal after its kind, every creeping thing that creeps on the earth after its kind, and every bird after its kind, everything with wings. 15Pairs of all creatures that have the breath of life came into the ark to Noah. 16Those that entered were male and female, just as God commanded him. Then the Lord shut him in.

17The flood engulfed the earth for forty days. As the waters increased, they lifted the ark and raised it above the earth. 18The waters completely overwhelmed the earth, and the ark floated on the surface of the waters. 19The waters completely inundated the earth so that even all the high mountains under the entire sky were covered. 20The waters rose more than 20 feet above the mountains. 21And all living things that moved on the earth died, including the birds, domestic animals, wild animals, all the creatures that swarm over the earth, and all humankind. 22Everything on dry land that had the breath of life in its nostrils died. 23So the Lord destroyed every living thing that was on the surface of the ground, including people, animals, creatures that creep along the ground, and birds of the sky. They were wiped off the earth. Only Noah and those who were with him in the ark survived. 24The waters prevailed over the earth for 150 days.

elements.question: What happens in the flood, and who survives?
elements.questionHint:
Look at the words used for how far the water reaches.
Look at who is left alive.
elements.sampleAnswer: The waters come from the deep and from the sky, and they rise until all the high mountains under the entire sky are covered. Every living thing that moved on the dry land died, including people, animals and birds. Only Noah and those with him in the ark survived. When they have entered, the Lord Himself shuts the door behind Noah.
elements.mainPoint: Judgement is **total**, and the only safety is the ark that God provides: the Lord Himself shuts the door.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: Genesis 6 described a world where every inclination was evil. Does the scale of the flood seem proportionate to you? What does it show about how seriously God takes sin?

elements.text: ‘But God remembered Noah’

At the height of the flood, the story turns on a single sentence in Genesis 8:1: “But God remembered Noah.” This does not mean God had forgotten him. In the Bible, to “remember” someone is to act on their behalf. Tap the reference on the next question to read what God does next.

elements.passageText: 1But God remembered Noah and all the wild animals and domestic animals that were with him in the ark. God caused a wind to blow over the earth and the waters receded.

elements.question: What does it mean that God “remembered” Noah, and what does He do next?
elements.questionHint: Look at what God does immediately after He remembers.
elements.sampleAnswer: God had not forgotten Noah. In the Bible, to remember someone is to act faithfully on their behalf. Verse 1 shows it straight away: God causes a wind to blow over the earth, and the waters recede. Even in the middle of judgement, God keeps faith with those He has saved.
elements.mainPoint: When Scripture says God **remembers**, He acts: He turns towards Noah and the waters begin to recede.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: Can you think of a time when circumstances felt overwhelming, yet in hindsight you can see God was at work?

elements.text: A new beginning, and a covenant

When Noah and his family leave the ark, his first act is worship. Then God speaks — and makes a promise. Not just to Noah, but to every living creature. Never again will a flood destroy the earth. And the sign of that promise is a rainbow in the clouds.

elements.passageText:
20Noah built an altar to the Lord. He then took some of every kind of clean animal and clean bird and offered burnt offerings on the altar. 21And the Lord smelled the soothing aroma and said to himself, “I will never again curse the ground because of humankind, even though the inclination of their minds is evil from childhood on. I will never again destroy everything that lives, as I have just done.

22“While the earth continues to exist,
planting time and harvest,
cold and heat,
summer and winter,
and day and night will not cease.”

elements.question: How does Noah respond when he leaves the ark, and what does the Lord promise?
elements.questionHint: Notice Noah’s first action, then the Lord’s promise in verses 21–22.
elements.sampleAnswer: Noah’s first act is to build an altar and offer burnt offerings: he worships before doing anything else. The Lord is pleased and resolves never again to curse the ground or destroy everything that lives. He says this even though human inclination is evil from childhood on, so the promise does not depend on people having improved. He also promises that planting and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter will not cease.
elements.mainPoint: Noah’s first act is **worship**, and God promises never again to destroy the earth, even though human hearts are still inclined to evil.

elements.passageText:
8God said to Noah and his sons, 9“Look. I now confirm my covenant with you and your descendants after you 10and with every living creature that is with you, including the birds, the domestic animals, and every living creature of the earth with you, all those that came out of the ark with you—every living creature of the earth. 11I confirm my covenant with you: Never again will all living things be wiped out by the waters of a flood; never again will a flood destroy the earth.”

12And God said, “This is the guarantee of the covenant I am making with you and every living creature with you, a covenant for all subsequent generations: 13I will place my rainbow in the clouds, and it will become a guarantee of the covenant between me and the earth. 14Whenever I bring clouds over the earth and the rainbow appears in the clouds, 15then I will remember my covenant with you and with all living creatures of all kinds. Never again will the waters become a flood and destroy all living things. 16When the rainbow is in the clouds, I will notice it and remember the perpetual covenant between God and all living creatures of all kinds that are on the earth.”

17So God said to Noah, “This is the guarantee of the covenant that I am confirming between me and all living things that are on the earth.”

elements.question: What does God promise, who is included, and what is the sign?
elements.questionHint:
Notice who is included in verses 9–10.
Notice what God places in the clouds.
elements.sampleAnswer: God confirms a covenant with Noah and his descendants, and with every living creature that was in the ark. The promise is that never again will a flood destroy the earth. The sign is a rainbow in the clouds, a reminder of the covenant for all later generations. God says that when He sees the rainbow, He will remember the covenant.
elements.mainPoint: God binds Himself by a **covenant** with Noah and every living creature: never again a flood, with the rainbow as the sign.

elements.text: A covenant is not just a promise — it is a binding commitment. God is not keeping His options open. He is making Himself accountable to His own word. This is the kind of God Genesis is introducing us to: not unpredictable or capricious, but faithful.

elements.question: What does the fact that God makes a covenant suggest about His character?
elements.questionHint:
Notice how often God says “I” in these verses.
Notice what He promises to remember.
elements.sampleAnswer: God takes the initiative: He confirms the covenant, places the rainbow, and promises to remember. He binds Himself to a promise and stakes His integrity on keeping it. The covenant covers all living creatures, so it is generous as well as firm. This shows a God who is faithful and trustworthy, not arbitrary or unpredictable.
elements.mainPoint: A God who makes a covenant is a God who **commits Himself**: His word can be trusted.

elements.text: Reflection Questions

elements.question: Do I tend to think more about God’s judgement or His grace? How does this passage hold both together?
In what area of my life do I need to trust and obey God more?
How have I experienced God’s patience or faithfulness in my own life?

elements.text: Prayer Focus

• Thank God for His mercy and patience
  • Acknowledge that He is holy and that sin has real consequences
  • Ask for faith to trust and obey Him
  • Thank Him that He makes promises and keeps them

‘God, thank You for Your mercy. Help me to trust You, obey You, and remember that You are both just and loving.’
This Week

Choose at least one:
  • Obey God in one area you have been delaying
  • Reflect on how God has shown mercy or patience in your own life — and thank Him
  • Trust God with something that feels uncertain or beyond your control
  • Let the image of the rainbow remind you, each time you see one, of God’s faithfulness

chapters.chapterTitle: Pride and Dispersion – The Tower of Babel

elements.text:
After the flood, humanity has a fresh start. The earth is renewed; the slate has been wiped clean. God’s instruction is clear: fill the earth, spread out, multiply. But it doesn’t take long for the same old pattern to re-emerge. People gather together – which is not itself wrong – but their goal reveals everything. They do not want to fill the earth. They want to make a name for themselves.

The Tower of Babel is not primarily a story about a building. It is a story about what happens when human ambition displaces God. Sin has now spread from one couple to a family, to a society, and to the nations. Babel is where it reaches the whole human race.

elements.question: It’s worth reading the whole passage before you begin...
elements.answer:
1This is the account of Noah’s sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Sons were born to them after the flood.

2The sons of Japheth were Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras. 3The sons of Gomer were Ashkenaz, Riphath, and Togarmah. 4The sons of Javan were Elishah, Tarshish, the Kittim, and the Dodanim. 5From these the coastlands of the nations were separated into their lands, every one according to its language, according to their families, by their nations.

6The sons of Ham were Cush, Mizraim, Put, and Canaan. 7The sons of Cush were Seba, Havilah, Sabtah, Raamah, and Sabteca. The sons of Raamah were Sheba and Dedan.

8Cush was the father of Nimrod; he began to be a valiant warrior on the earth. 9He was a mighty hunter before the Lord. (That is why it is said, “Like Nimrod, a mighty hunter before the Lord.”) 10The primary regions of his kingdom were Babel, Erech, Akkad, and Calneh in the land of Shinar. 11From that land he went to Assyria, where he built Nineveh, Rehoboth Ir, Calah, 12and Resen, which is between Nineveh and the great city Calah.

13Mizraim was the father of the Ludites, Anamites, Lehabites, Naphtuhites, 14Pathrusites, Casluhites (from whom the Philistines came), and Caphtorites.

15Canaan was the father of Sidon his firstborn, Heth, 16the Jebusites, Amorites, Girgashites, 17Hivites, Arkites, Sinites, 18Arvadites, Zemarites, and Hamathites. Eventually the families of the Canaanites were scattered 19and the borders of Canaan extended from Sidon all the way to Gerar as far as Gaza, and all the way to Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboyim, as far as Lasha. 20These are the sons of Ham, according to their families, according to their languages, by their lands, and by their nations.

21And sons were also born to Shem (the older brother of Japheth), the father of all the sons of Eber.

22The sons of Shem were Elam, Asshur, Arphaxad, Lud, and Aram. 23The sons of Aram were Uz, Hul, Gether, and Mash. 24Arphaxad was the father of Shelah, and Shelah was the father of Eber. 25Two sons were born to Eber: One was named Peleg because in his days the earth was divided, and his brother’s name was Joktan. 26Joktan was the father of Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah, 27Hadoram, Uzal, Diklah, 28Obal, Abimael, Sheba, 29Ophir, Havilah, and Jobab. All these were sons of Joktan. 30Their dwelling place was from Mesha all the way to Sephar in the eastern hills. 31These are the sons of Shem according to their families, according to their languages, by their lands, and according to their nations.

32These are the families of the sons of Noah, according to their genealogies, by their nations, and from these the nations spread over the earth after the flood.

11:1The whole earth had a common language and a common vocabulary. 11:2When the people moved eastward, they found a plain in Shinar and settled there. 11:3Then they said to one another, “Come, let’s make bricks and bake them thoroughly.” (They had brick instead of stone and tar instead of mortar.) 11:4Then they said, “Come, let’s build ourselves a city and a tower with its top in the heavens so that we may make a name for ourselves. Otherwise we will be scattered across the face of the entire earth.”

11:5But the Lord came down to see the city and the tower that the people had started building. 11:6And the Lord said, “If as one people all sharing a common language they have begun to do this, then nothing they plan to do will be beyond them. 11:7Come, let’s go down and confuse their language so they won’t be able to understand each other.”

11:8So the Lord scattered them from there across the face of the entire earth, and they stopped building the city. 11:9That is why its name was called Babel —because there the Lord confused the language of the entire world, and from there the Lord scattered them across the face of the entire earth.

NET – see context ↗

elements.text: The nations spread, as God intended

Genesis 10 is often called the Table of Nations: a long list tracing how Noah’s descendants spread into different families, lands and languages. It can be tiring to read, but the point is significant. After the flood God told Noah’s family to fill the earth (Genesis 9:1), and this chapter shows the nations spreading out across it.

elements.passageText:
1Then God blessed Noah and his sons and said to them, “Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth.

10:1This is the account of Noah’s sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Sons were born to them after the flood.

10:2The sons of Japheth were Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras. 10:3The sons of Gomer were Ashkenaz, Riphath, and Togarmah. 10:4The sons of Javan were Elishah, Tarshish, the Kittim, and the Dodanim. 10:5From these the coastlands of the nations were separated into their lands, every one according to its language, according to their families, by their nations.

10:31These are the sons of Shem according to their families, according to their languages, by their lands, and according to their nations.

10:32These are the families of the sons of Noah, according to their genealogies, by their nations, and from these the nations spread over the earth after the flood.

elements.question: God told Noah’s family to “fill the earth” (9:1). What does Genesis 10 describe happening?
elements.questionHint: Look at the repeated words “families”, “languages”, “lands” and “nations”.
elements.sampleAnswer: Genesis 10 traces the descendants of Noah’s three sons as they spread out into different lands, by their families, languages and nations. It ends by saying that from these families the nations spread over the earth after the flood. This is the kind of spreading God had commanded in 9:1: Noah’s family is filling the earth.
elements.mainPoint: Genesis 10 shows God’s command to **fill the earth** being fulfilled: nations, languages and lands spreading out from Noah’s family.

elements.text: One people, one goal

Then the scene shifts. In Genesis 11, we are told that the whole world has one language, and people are moving together. They settle in a plain and begin to make plans.
“Come, let’s build ourselves a city and a tower with its top in the heavens so that we may make a name for ourselves. Otherwise we will be scattered across the face of the entire earth.” (Genesis 11:4, NET)
Notice what drives them: the fear of being scattered, and the desire to be known – to have a name, to be significant, to leave a mark. These are not alien desires. They are deeply human. But they are being pursued without any reference to God, and in direct resistance to what God had told them to do.

elements.passageText:
1Then God blessed Noah and his sons and said to them, “Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth.

11:1The whole earth had a common language and a common vocabulary. 11:2When the people moved eastward, they found a plain in Shinar and settled there. 11:3Then they said to one another, “Come, let’s make bricks and bake them thoroughly.” (They had brick instead of stone and tar instead of mortar.) 11:4Then they said, “Come, let’s build ourselves a city and a tower with its top in the heavens so that we may make a name for ourselves. Otherwise we will be scattered across the face of the entire earth.”

elements.question: What do the people say they want to do in verses 3–4, and what two reasons do they give?
elements.questionHint:
Look at what they want to build.
Look at the phrases “make a name” and “otherwise”.
elements.sampleAnswer: They make bricks and decide to build a city and a tower with its top in the heavens. They give two reasons: “so that we may make a name for ourselves”, and “otherwise we will be scattered across the face of the entire earth”. The first is about self-made significance and glory; the second is about security. Both put their own plans at the centre.
elements.mainPoint: Babel’s builders want **a name for themselves** and security without God: their goal is their own glory.

elements.question: How does what the people say in 11:4 compare with what God told Noah’s family in 9:1?
elements.questionHint: Compare “fill the earth” with “otherwise we will be scattered”.
elements.sampleAnswer: God told them to fill the earth, which means spreading out. The people at Babel gather in one place and say they must build a city so that they will not be scattered. They are choosing to stay together, to avoid doing the very thing God had told them to do. And their reason is to make a name for themselves, not to honour God.
elements.mainPoint: Babel is a **rebellion against God’s instruction**: they gather to avoid doing exactly what He said, for their own glory.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: People today still try to make “a name” for themselves, through status, success or recognition. Where do you see it? (The book describes people seeking a false honour to cover their shame, “like the builders of Babel”.)

elements.text: At the heart of Babel is pride – the conviction that human effort and human unity can achieve significance without God. It echoes Genesis 3: the same impulse to reach beyond what God has given, to secure for themselves what only God can truly provide.
God comes down

What is darkly comic about this passage is God’s response. The tower the people are building, the one with its top ‘in the heavens’ – God has to come down to see it. The gap between their ambition and reality is enormous.
“…nothing they plan to do will be beyond them.” (Genesis 11:6, NET)
This sounds like a compliment, but it isn’t. God sees where this road leads – not to human flourishing, but to ever-greater self-assertion and rebellion. He acts to interrupt the project.

elements.passageText: 5But the Lord came down to see the city and the tower that the people had started building. 6And the Lord said, “If as one people all sharing a common language they have begun to do this, then nothing they plan to do will be beyond them. 7Come, let’s go down and confuse their language so they won’t be able to understand each other.”

elements.question: How does the Lord respond to what the people are building?
elements.questionHint:
Notice where the Lord goes.
Notice what He says in verse 6.
Notice what He plans in verse 7.
elements.sampleAnswer: The Lord comes down to see the city and the tower. The tower with its top “in the heavens” is so small beside Him that He has to come down to see it. He says that if as one people sharing a language they have begun this, nothing they plan to do will be beyond them. So He plans to confuse their language so that they cannot understand each other, which limits where unchecked pride would lead.
elements.mainPoint: Their towering ambition is small beside God: He **comes down** to see it, and acts to limit where unchecked pride would lead.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: The builders had unity, a shared language and skill. What does God’s intervention teach about the limits of human power?

elements.text: Scattered

What they feared most – being scattered – is exactly what happens. The irony is complete. They tried to resist God’s instruction to spread out, and the consequence is that they are scattered. Their attempt to secure themselves through unity and ambition ends in fragmentation.

elements.passageText:
1Then God blessed Noah and his sons and said to them, “Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth.

11:8So the Lord scattered them from there across the face of the entire earth, and they stopped building the city. 11:9That is why its name was called Babel —because there the Lord confused the language of the entire world, and from there the Lord scattered them across the face of the entire earth.

elements.question: What happens at the end of the story (verses 8–9), and how does it compare with what God had said in 9:1?
elements.questionHint: Compare what the people feared with what the Lord does.
elements.sampleAnswer: The Lord scatters them across the face of the entire earth, and they stop building the city. The place is called Babel because there the Lord confused the language of the entire world. What they feared and tried to avoid is exactly what happens. And in the process God’s instruction to fill the earth is carried out anyway.
elements.mainPoint: What they feared happens, and **God’s purpose stands**: resisting Him brings the very outcome they tried to avoid.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: What do you think we find when we resist God’s will, drawing on what happened at Babel?

elements.text: Reflection Questions

elements.question: Where do I see pride in my own life?
Do I tend to rely more on myself or on God? What does that look like in practice?
Is there a plan or ambition I need to surrender to God?

elements.text: Prayer Focus

• Ask God to reveal any pride you have been carrying
  • Pray for genuine humility and dependence on Him
  • Surrender your plans and ambitions to God
  • Ask Him to help you live for His glory, not your own
‘God, help me not to live for myself, but for You. Teach me humility, and help me to trust Your plan for my life.’
This Week

Choose at least one:
  • Identify one area where you seek recognition, control, or significance – and bring it to God in prayer
  • Do something good for someone without telling anyone about it
  • Before making a decision this week, pause and ask: ‘Is this for my glory or God’s?’
  • Surrender one personal plan or ambition to God

chapters.chapterTitle: God’s Call – The Beginning of Redemption

elements.text:
Genesis 1-11 has established a dispiriting pattern. God creates something good. Humanity turns away from Him. Consequences follow. God shows mercy. And the cycle begins again – each time reaching new depths of rebellion. Creation, fall, flood, Babel. It could continue indefinitely.

Then, in Genesis 12, something changes. God makes a move that is different in kind from anything that has come before. He doesn’t simply judge or restrain. He calls. He chooses one man, makes him extraordinary promises, and sets in motion a plan that will – as we will eventually discover – reach to the ends of the earth. What began with one couple has spread to a family, to a society and to the nations; God’s answer is a promise to bless all of them.

elements.question: It’s worth reading the whole passage before you begin...
elements.answer:
10This is the account of Shem.

Shem was 100 years old when he became the father of Arphaxad, two years after the flood. 11And after becoming the father of Arphaxad, Shem lived 500 years and had other sons and daughters.

12When Arphaxad had lived 35 years, he became the father of Shelah. 13And after he became the father of Shelah, Arphaxad lived 403 years and had other sons and daughters.

14When Shelah had lived 30 years, he became the father of Eber. 15And after he became the father of Eber, Shelah lived 403 years and had other sons and daughters.

16When Eber had lived 34 years, he became the father of Peleg. 17And after he became the father of Peleg, Eber lived 430 years and had other sons and daughters.

18When Peleg had lived 30 years, he became the father of Reu. 19And after he became the father of Reu, Peleg lived 209 years and had other sons and daughters.

20When Reu had lived 32 years, he became the father of Serug. 21And after he became the father of Serug, Reu lived 207 years and had other sons and daughters.

22When Serug had lived 30 years, he became the father of Nahor. 23And after he became the father of Nahor, Serug lived 200 years and had other sons and daughters.

24When Nahor had lived 29 years, he became the father of Terah. 25And after he became the father of Terah, Nahor lived 119 years and had other sons and daughters.

26When Terah had lived 70 years, he became the father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran.

27This is the account of Terah.

Terah became the father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran. And Haran became the father of Lot. 28Haran died in the land of his birth, in Ur of the Chaldeans, while his father Terah was still alive. 29And Abram and Nahor took wives for themselves. The name of Abram’s wife was Sarai. And the name of Nahor’s wife was Milcah; she was the daughter of Haran, who was the father of both Milcah and Iscah. 30But Sarai was barren; she had no children.

31Terah took his son Abram, his grandson Lot (the son of Haran), and his daughter-in-law Sarai, his son Abram’s wife, and with them he set out from Ur of the Chaldeans to go to Canaan. When they came to Haran, they settled there. 32The lifetime of Terah was 205 years, and he died in Haran.

12:1Now the Lord said to Abram,

“Go out from your country, your relatives, and your father’s household
to the land that I will show you.
12:2Then I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless you,
and I will make your name great,
so that you will exemplify divine blessing.
12:3I will bless those who bless you,
but the one who treats you lightly I must curse,
so that all the families of the earth may receive blessing through you.”

12:4So Abram left, just as the Lord had told him to do, and Lot went with him. (Now Abram was 75 years old when he departed from Haran.) 12:5And Abram took his wife Sarai, his nephew Lot, and all the possessions they had accumulated and the people they had acquired in Haran, and they left for the land of Canaan. They entered the land of Canaan.

12:6Abram traveled through the land as far as the oak tree of Moreh at Shechem. (At that time the Canaanites were in the land.) 12:7The Lord appeared to Abram and said, “To your descendants I will give this land.” So Abram built an altar there to the Lord, who had appeared to him.

12:8Then he moved from there to the hill country east of Bethel and pitched his tent, with Bethel on the west and Ai on the east. There he built an altar to the Lord and worshiped the Lord. 12:9Abram continually journeyed by stages down to the Negev.

NET – see context ↗

elements.text: A family line God has been tracking

Before we meet Abram, Genesis traces a genealogy from Shem – one of Noah’s sons – down through the generations to a man called Terah, and his son Abram. It may seem like routine record-keeping, but it is more than that. God has been at work through history, quietly preserving a line of people through whom His plan will unfold.

elements.passageText:
10This is the account of Shem.

Shem was 100 years old when he became the father of Arphaxad, two years after the flood. 11And after becoming the father of Arphaxad, Shem lived 500 years and had other sons and daughters.

12When Arphaxad had lived 35 years, he became the father of Shelah. 13And after he became the father of Shelah, Arphaxad lived 403 years and had other sons and daughters.

14When Shelah had lived 30 years, he became the father of Eber. 15And after he became the father of Eber, Shelah lived 403 years and had other sons and daughters.

16When Eber had lived 34 years, he became the father of Peleg. 17And after he became the father of Peleg, Eber lived 430 years and had other sons and daughters.

18When Peleg had lived 30 years, he became the father of Reu. 19And after he became the father of Reu, Peleg lived 209 years and had other sons and daughters.

20When Reu had lived 32 years, he became the father of Serug. 21And after he became the father of Serug, Reu lived 207 years and had other sons and daughters.

22When Serug had lived 30 years, he became the father of Nahor. 23And after he became the father of Nahor, Serug lived 200 years and had other sons and daughters.

24When Nahor had lived 29 years, he became the father of Terah. 25And after he became the father of Terah, Nahor lived 119 years and had other sons and daughters.

26When Terah had lived 70 years, he became the father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran.

elements.question: What is this genealogy tracing, and where does it lead?
elements.questionHint: Follow the line of names from Shem to Terah, and notice who is named last.
elements.sampleAnswer: The genealogy traces a single family line from Shem, one of Noah’s sons, through a series of generations to Terah and his sons, ending with Abram. The line runs without a break through ordinary births and deaths. It leads the story from the whole world (Genesis 10–11) to one family, and to one man, Abram.
elements.mainPoint: The genealogy **narrows the story**: through ordinary generations, the line runs from Shem to Abram.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: Genesis 3:15 promised an offspring who would defeat the serpent. How might a list like this keep that promise in view?

elements.text: An ordinary man

When we first encounter Abram, there is nothing obviously special about him. He has a family. He lives in a specific place. His wife Sarai is unable to have children – a detail that will become deeply significant, since God’s promise will involve a great nation descending from this couple.

elements.passageText:
27This is the account of Terah.

Terah became the father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran. And Haran became the father of Lot. 28Haran died in the land of his birth, in Ur of the Chaldeans, while his father Terah was still alive. 29And Abram and Nahor took wives for themselves. The name of Abram’s wife was Sarai. And the name of Nahor’s wife was Milcah; she was the daughter of Haran, who was the father of both Milcah and Iscah. 30But Sarai was barren; she had no children.

31Terah took his son Abram, his grandson Lot (the son of Haran), and his daughter-in-law Sarai, his son Abram’s wife, and with them he set out from Ur of the Chaldeans to go to Canaan. When they came to Haran, they settled there. 32The lifetime of Terah was 205 years, and he died in Haran.

elements.question: What do we learn about Abram’s family and situation at the start?
elements.questionHint:
Notice what verse 30 says about Sarai.
Notice where the family has stopped.
elements.sampleAnswer: Abram is part of Terah’s family, with his wife Sarai and his nephew Lot. His brother Haran died in Ur. Terah set out with them for Canaan, but they settled in Haran, where Terah died. Verse 30 adds that Sarai was barren and had no children. So Abram is an ordinary man with a family, but with no heir.
elements.mainPoint: Abram is an **ordinary man without an heir**: Sarai is barren, and the family has settled short of Canaan.

elements.text: God takes the initiative

The call, when it comes, is remarkable in its simplicity and its demand:
“Go out from your country, your relatives, and your father’s household to the land that I will show you.” (Genesis 12:1, NET)
God doesn’t tell Abram where he is going. He just tells him to go. This is not a plan that Abram can evaluate on its merits – it requires trust in the one giving the instruction.

elements.passageText:
30But Sarai was barren; she had no children.

12:1Now the Lord said to Abram,

“Go out from your country, your relatives, and your father’s household
to the land that I will show you.
12:2Then I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless you,
and I will make your name great,
so that you will exemplify divine blessing.
12:3I will bless those who bless you,
but the one who treats you lightly I must curse,
so that all the families of the earth may receive blessing through you.”

elements.question: What does God ask Abram to leave, and what does He tell him about where he is going?
elements.questionHint: List the three things Abram is told to leave, then notice what God says about the destination.
elements.sampleAnswer: God tells Abram to go out from his country, his relatives and his father’s household. These are the sources of security and identity in the ancient world. The destination is only “the land that I will show you”: no name and no map. Abram is asked to go on the strength of God’s word alone.
elements.mainPoint: God asks Abram to **leave everything familiar** and go to a land he has not yet been shown.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: What would you want to know before leaving everything? How much of that does Abram receive?

elements.text: A promise that spans the world

But God doesn’t just issue a command. He makes promises – extraordinary ones.
“I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless you… so that all the families of the earth may receive blessing through you.” (Genesis 12:2–3, NET)
The scope of this promise is astonishing. It begins with one man and reaches to all the families of the earth. This is the first clear signal in Genesis that God’s plan is not just for one family, or one nation – it is for everyone. What begins here will eventually unfold across the entire Bible.

elements.question: What does God promise Abram in verses 2–3?
elements.questionHint: Notice the repeated “I will” and the final purpose in verse 3.
elements.sampleAnswer: God promises to make Abram into a great nation and to bless him. He will make his name great, so that Abram will exemplify divine blessing. God will bless those who bless Abram and curse the one who treats him lightly. And the goal is wider than Abram: so that all the families of the earth may receive blessing through him.
keyTerms: all|families of the earth|every nation|through you
elements.mainPoint: God promises Abram a **great nation and blessing**, and the final goal is that all the families of the earth may receive blessing through him.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: The promise begins with one man and ends with “all the families of the earth”. What does that suggest about who God is ultimately concerned for?

elements.question: Sarai was barren (11:30), and God promises Abram a great nation. What does the passage emphasise about who will make that promise happen?
elements.questionHint:
Count the “I will” statements in verses 2–3.
Ask who is doing the acting.
elements.sampleAnswer: God makes the promises: “I will make you into a great nation”, “I will bless you”, “I will make your name great”, “I will bless those who bless you”. Abram has a barren wife and no children, so a great nation cannot come from his own strength. The only thing asked of Abram is that he go. The promise rests on what God will do.
elements.mainPoint: The promise rests on **what God will do**, not on Abram’s ability: a barren couple will become a great nation only because God says so.

elements.text: Abram goes

The response is straightforward:
“So Abram left, just as the Lord had told him to do, and Lot went with him.” (Genesis 12:4, NET)
No recorded hesitation. No list of conditions. He goes. He takes his family and his possessions and he leaves – for a land he has not yet seen, trusting a God whose instructions have given him almost no detail about what lies ahead. This is what faith looks like: not certainty about the outcome, but confidence in the one who gives the promise.

elements.passageText: 4So Abram left, just as the Lord had told him to do, and Lot went with him. (Now Abram was 75 years old when he departed from Haran.) 5And Abram took his wife Sarai, his nephew Lot, and all the possessions they had accumulated and the people they had acquired in Haran, and they left for the land of Canaan. They entered the land of Canaan.

elements.question: How does Abram respond in verses 4–5, and what does he take with him?
elements.questionHint: Notice the first words of verse 4 and the list of what Abram takes.
elements.sampleAnswer: “So Abram left, just as the Lord had told him to do.” There is no recorded hesitation and no negotiation. He takes Sarai, his nephew Lot, all their possessions and the people they had acquired in Haran, and sets out for Canaan. He is 75 years old. His faith is shown in action, not in words.
elements.mainPoint: Abram **simply goes**, just as the Lord told him: faith shown in obedience.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: What might have held Abram back (his age, his barren wife, no destination)? What does it mean that he went anyway?

elements.text: Worship along the way

As Abram travels through the land, he builds altars. This is not incidental. In the middle of an uncertain journey, in a land that is not yet his, he keeps stopping to acknowledge God. His faith is not just a one-time decision – it is expressed repeatedly, in worship, as he goes.

elements.passageText:
6Abram traveled through the land as far as the oak tree of Moreh at Shechem. (At that time the Canaanites were in the land.) 7The Lord appeared to Abram and said, “To your descendants I will give this land.” So Abram built an altar there to the Lord, who had appeared to him.

8Then he moved from there to the hill country east of Bethel and pitched his tent, with Bethel on the west and Ai on the east. There he built an altar to the Lord and worshiped the Lord. 9Abram continually journeyed by stages down to the Negev.

elements.question: What does Abram do as he travels through the land, and what does the Lord tell him at Shechem?
elements.questionHint:
Look for the places Abram stops.
Look for what he builds.
elements.sampleAnswer: At Shechem the Lord appears and says “To your descendants I will give this land”, and Abram builds an altar to Him. He then moves to the hill country east of Bethel, pitches his tent, and builds another altar, where he worships the Lord. All the while the Canaanites are in the land, so it is not yet his. He keeps stopping to worship as he goes.
elements.mainPoint: Abram **worships as he goes**, building altars in a land that is not yet his, trusting God’s promise.

deeper.label: Go deeper …
deeper.question: How can you stay connected to God in the midst of change or uncertainty in your own life? What did Abram actually do?

elements.text: Reflection Questions

elements.question: What stands out to me about God’s call to Abram?
Is trusting God easy or difficult for me? What makes the difference?
What might God be calling me to trust Him with right now?

elements.text: Prayer Focus

• Thank God for His plan to restore and bless – a plan that reaches to all people
  • Ask Him to help you trust Him more
  • Pray for courage to obey in areas where you feel uncertain
  • Surrender your future to God
‘God, help me to trust You like Abram did. Lead me, and give me the courage to follow You wherever You call me.’
This Week

Choose at least one:
  • Take one step of obedience in an area where you sense God is prompting you
  • Trust God with something that currently feels uncertain
  • Write down what you sense God is leading you toward
  • Spend time simply asking: ‘God, what are You calling me to?’
